newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Punjab is peaceful, but investors shy away.
newsitem.headline: India's Punjab is peaceful, but investors shy away.

text.p: Industries are buzzing again in India's farming state of Punjab after an end to years of separatist violence, but businessmen said on Thursday that foreign investors were still staying away for other reasons.

As the state prepared to elect a new local government on Friday in the first poll in two decades not overshadowed by a bloody Sikh revolt, businessmen said they were worried about the capacity of the new government to sustain fiscal discipline.

"If the Akali Dal wins, as is being predicted, their economic policies could be disastrous for the state," Pitambar Datt Sharma, president of Punjab's Apex Chambers of Commerce and Industry, told Reuters.
The Akali Dal, which has considerable support among rich Sikh landowners, could end up pleasing them at the cost of urban industries, businessmen said.

Most opinion polls say the Akali Dal of former chief minister Prakash Singh Badal, which was once seen as flirting with separatists, would replace the Congress party's government in the polls. Results are expected by Sunday.
The Congress won local elections in heavily-guarded voting held in 1992, months after its own federal government kickstarted a free-market programme.
But its opportunities bypassed Punjab, which saw 20,000 deaths over a decade of separatism.

Sharma said the Congress had its share of populist measures but the Akali Dal, which rests on bedrock support among rural Sikhs, had promised to allow free water and electricity to certain categories of farmers.
"If that happens the state would lose 10 billion rupees ($ 27.9 million) a year on revenue," Sharma said. "This kind of competitive populism has only added to Punjab's anti-investor attitude."
The Akali Dal is fighting the elections in alliance with India's main opposition rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which has a base among the state's mostly urban Hindus.
Decades of Sikh separatism had fuelled considerable mistrust among Punjab's two main communities, Sharma said.

"My fear is that the Akali government may want to transfer the burden of rural subsidies to industry, which could lead to an urban-rural divide," Sharma said. "Given the demographic nature of the two communities, it could revive communalism among them."
The government says while industrial investment had risen between 1993 and 1996 by 38 percent, production had gone up by 85 percent and exports grew by 73 percent.
However, apart from a unit of the United States-based PepsiCo which opened a plant here three years ago, the state has not been able to attract any major foreign firms.
But the state wants to increase urban employment.

"The idea is to increase the present share of industry in GDP (gross domestic product) to 25 percent from 17 percent," a state official said. "We also propose to step up the annual industrial growth to 12 percent from the present eight percent in two years."

"As far as we can see, the days of militancy are over. It could take a bit longer for foreign investors to realise that," said P.K. Rajgarhia, former president of the PHD (Punjab, Haryana, Delhi) Chamber of Commerce and Industry.
Businessmen said the state, regarded as India's food basket, needed more investments in infrastructure, including better air and rail links and a container depot.

"There is a lot of potential to expand Punjab's industry," said Harinder Pal Bhogal, a Ludhiana-based industrialist in the border state. "The question is, is that the priority of the new government?" ($1=35.8 rupees)
